title: 67% of Caregivers Feel Mentally Exhausted
paragraphs: Looking after an aging parent or relative can be rewarding, but it can also be extremely draining. According to a new survey in the United States, two-thirds of people who care for aging family members feel that they have reached their mental limit.

The survey was carried out by Talker Research for Visiting Angels, a company that provides care for elderly people in their homes. It asked 2,000 American adults about their daily lives in August 2026.

The survey focused on the idea of "mental load," which refers to all the behind-the-scenes work of keeping a life running, such as planning, organizing and remembering things. Overall, 54% of respondents said that their mental load was at maximum capacity during a typical week. Among people who were currently caring for an aging family member, this figure rose to 67%.

For many people, caregiving came as a surprise. Around 62% of current and former caregivers said that they had to start suddenly because of an urgent need, and only 26% had planned for it. As a result, many felt unprepared. Around 31% said they were not ready financially, while 23% said they were not ready mentally and 22% said they were not ready emotionally.

Caregiving also forced many people to make sacrifices. Around 36% said they had cut back on time for themselves, and 29% said they had reduced their social lives. Furthermore, 27% admitted that they had stopped making their own mental health a priority, while 21% had neglected their physical health.
Some caregivers are also raising children at the same time. Many of these people said they felt guilty, whether they were spending time with their children or with their aging relatives.

Caregivers who took part in the survey offered advice to others. One said that burnout is real and that caregivers cannot do everything alone. Another suggested finding a little time for yourself every day.
It should be noted that the survey was commissioned by a company that sells care services.
